expectedText:
EMPLOYEE'S REQUEST TO INSPECT PERSONNEL AND PAYROLL RECORDS
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

REQUEST TO INSPECT AND COPY RECORDS
This is a written request from Jordan Lee to Acme, Inc., submitted on September 1, 2026. As of the date of this request, Jordan Lee's employment status is: Former employee (employment ended August 15, 2026).

Jordan Lee requests the following records: Complete personnel file, including performance evaluations, and payroll records for the last three years of employment.

This request references rights described under California Labor Code sections 1198.5 and 226, addressed in the informational sections of this document. Nothing in this letter is a claim that any particular record exists in Acme, Inc.'s files, or a demand for records beyond what California law makes available under those statutes.

TWO SEPARATE STATUTORY RIGHTS: PERSONNEL RECORDS AND PAYROLL RECORDS
California law recognizes two separate statutory rights that let Jordan Lee inspect and obtain copies of employment-related records held by Acme, Inc. Labor Code § 1198.5 gives every current and former employee, or their representative, the right to inspect and receive a copy of the personnel records the employer maintains relating to the employee's performance, including education or training records, or to any grievance concerning the employee; an employer receiving a written request under § 1198.5 must make those records available no later than 30 calendar days from the date of the request (or up to 35 calendar days if the employee or representative and the employer agree in writing to a later date). Separately, Labor Code § 226(b)-(c) gives a current or former employee the right to inspect or receive a copy of records the employer is required to keep in connection with itemized wage statements — payroll records — and requires the employer to comply as soon as practicable but no later than 21 calendar days from the date of the request. These are two different statutes, reaching two different categories of records, with two different compliance deadlines; a request that names only one of the two statutes, or that describes only one category of records, does not automatically function as a request under the other.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Every current and former employee, or their representative, has the right to inspect and receive a copy of the personnel records that the employer maintains relating to the employee’s performance, including education or training records, or to any grievance concerning the employee."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1198.5(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1198.5.)
  "An employer who receives a written or oral request to inspect or receive a copy of records pursuant to subdivision (b) pertaining to a current or former employee shall comply with the request as soon as practicable, but no later than 21 calendar days from the date of the request."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 226(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=226.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's personnel/payroll records inspection rights — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or employee. The two citations below are to two different California statutes (Labor Code §§ 1198.5 and 226), not two subsections of the same statute, so no same-section duplication is being treated as two independent sources. This clause states the general distinction; it does not resolve, for a specific document a reader believes the employer holds, which of the two statutes (if either) actually covers that document — that depends on whether the document is a 'personnel record' relating to performance or a grievance under § 1198.5, a payroll record of the kind § 226(a) requires an employer to keep, both, or neither, none of which this clause determines. This document does not re-derive the full text or mechanics of the § 226 wage-statement itemization requirement itself, which this project's separate Wage Statement Itemization Policy document already covers in more detail.

WHO MAY REQUEST PERSONNEL RECORDS, AND HOW OFTEN
Labor Code § 1198.5 gives the right to inspect and copy personnel records to every current and former employee, or their representative — a right that is not limited to employees who are actively employed at the time of the request. A "representative," for these purposes, means a person Jordan Lee authorizes in writing to inspect or receive a copy of Jordan Lee's personnel records on Jordan Lee's behalf; Acme, Inc. may take reasonable steps to verify the identity of the current or former employee or authorized representative making the request. If Jordan Lee is a former employee of Acme, Inc., California law limits Acme, Inc.'s obligation to comply with more than one request per year from that former employee (or their representative) to inspect or receive a copy of personnel records.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Every current and former employee, or their representative, has the right to inspect and receive a copy of the personnel records that the employer maintains relating to the employee’s performance, including education or training records, or to any grievance concerning the employee."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1198.5(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1198.5.)
  "An employer is required to comply with only one request per year by a former employee to inspect or receive a copy of their personnel records."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1198.5(d) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1198.5.)
  "The employer may take reasonable steps to verify the identity of a current or former employee or their authorized representative. For purposes of this section, “representative” means a person authorized in writing by the employee to inspect, or receive a copy of, their personnel records."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1198.5(e) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1198.5.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's personnel/payroll records inspection rights — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or employee. The three citations below are to three different subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Labor Code § 1198.5 — subdivisions (a)(1), (d), and (e) — so they are treated as one source, not three independent ones. This clause does not address the statute's separate 50-request-per-calendar-month cap on requests filed by a representative or representatives of employees generally (§ 1198.5(p)), nor the statute's exemption for an employee covered by a qualifying collective bargaining agreement (§ 1198.5(q)); neither is quoted or relied on here.

THE RESPONSE TIMEFRAME UNDER § 1198.5: 30 CALENDAR DAYS, UP TO 35 BY WRITTEN AGREEMENT
Once Acme, Inc. receives a written request from Jordan Lee (or Jordan Lee's representative) to inspect personnel records covered by Labor Code § 1198.5, California law requires Acme, Inc. to make those records available for inspection no later than 30 calendar days from the date Acme, Inc. receives the request — unless Jordan Lee (or the representative) and Acme, Inc. agree in writing to a later date, which cannot exceed 35 calendar days from Acme, Inc.'s receipt of the request. The same 30-calendar-day deadline, extendable to 35 calendar days by the same kind of written agreement, applies separately to a request for a copy of the records. Where Acme, Inc. provides copies, California law lets Acme, Inc. charge Jordan Lee an amount not to exceed the actual cost of reproduction.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The employer shall make the contents of those personnel records available for inspection to the current or former employee, or their representative, at reasonable intervals and at reasonable times, but not later than 30 calendar days from the date the employer receives a written request, unless the current or former employee, or their representative, and the employer agree in writing to a date beyond 30 calendar days to inspect the records, and the agreed-upon date does not exceed 35 calendar days from the employer’s receipt of the written request. Upon a written request from a current or former employee, or their representative, the employer shall also provide a copy of the personnel records, at a charge not to exceed the actual cost of reproduction, not later than 30 calendar days from the date the employer receives the request, unless the current or former employee, or their representative, and the employer agree in writing to a date beyond 30 calendar days to produce a copy of the records, as long as the agreed-upon date does not exceed 35 calendar days from the employer’s receipt of the written request."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1198.5(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1198.5.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's personnel/payroll records inspection rights — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or employee. This clause is drawn from a single statutory subdivision, § 1198.5(b)(1); no additional independent source was sought for this specific point. That same subdivision also states that, except as provided in § 1198.5(c)(2), an employer is not required to make personnel records or a copy of them available at a time when the employee is actually required to render service to the employer, if the requester is the employee — a timing nuance this clause does not separately restate. This clause does not address the statute's distinct requirement (§ 1198.5(c)(1)) that an employer keep a copy of each employee's personnel records for at least three years after termination of employment, which bears on record retention rather than on the response deadline described here.

WHAT § 1198.5 DOES NOT REACH: STATUTORY EXCLUSIONS
Labor Code § 1198.5's inspection-and-copy right does not extend to every document that might exist somewhere in Jordan Lee's file at Acme, Inc. By its own terms, the statute does not apply to: records relating to the investigation of a possible criminal offense; letters of reference; and ratings, reports, or records that were obtained before Jordan Lee's employment began, prepared by identifiable examination committee members, or obtained in connection with a promotional examination. The statute also excludes two categories of employees from its coverage altogether: employees subject to the Public Safety Officers Procedural Bill of Rights, and employees of agencies subject to the Information Practices Act of 1977.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The requirements of this section do not apply to: (1) Records relating to the investigation of a possible criminal offense. (2) Letters of reference. (3) Ratings, reports, or records that were: (A) Obtained prior to the employee’s employment. (B) Prepared by identifiable examination committee members. (C) Obtained in connection with a promotional examination. (4) Employees who are subject to the Public Safety Officers Procedural Bill of Rights (Chapter 9.7 (commencing with Section 3300) of Division 4 of Title 1 of the Government Code). (5) Employees of agencies subject to the Information Practices Act of 1977 (Title 1.8 (commencing with Section 1798) of Part 4 of Division 3 of the Civil Code)."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1198.5(h) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1198.5.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's personnel/payroll records inspection rights — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or employee. This clause is drawn from a single statutory subdivision, § 1198.5(h) (paragraphs (1) through (5)); no additional independent source was sought for this exclusions list. Whether a specific document in the employee's personnel file actually falls within one of these exclusions — for example, whether a given report was in fact "obtained prior to the employee's employment" or instead prepared afterward — is a factual question this clause does not resolve.

THE SEPARATE PAYROLL-RECORDS RIGHT UNDER § 226, AND ITS 21-DAY DEADLINE
Separately from the personnel-records right described above, Labor Code § 226(b) gives Jordan Lee, as a current or former employee of Acme, Inc., the right to inspect or receive a copy of records pertaining to Jordan Lee's employment that Acme, Inc. is required to keep under the itemized-wage-statement statute — Acme, Inc.'s payroll records — upon reasonable request. Acme, Inc. may take reasonable steps to verify Jordan Lee's identity, and may charge Jordan Lee the actual cost of reproduction for copies. Acme, Inc. must comply with a request as soon as practicable but no later than 21 calendar days from the date of the request — a shorter deadline than the 30-to-35-calendar-day deadline that applies to a personnel-records request under § 1198.5. If Acme, Inc. fails to permit inspection or copying of payroll records within that 21-day window, California law lets Jordan Lee or the Labor Commissioner recover a $750 penalty from Acme, Inc. — the same dollar figure as the personnel-records penalty described elsewhere in this document, though the two $750 penalties arise under two different statutes and correspond to two different categories of records and two different deadlines.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "An employer that is required by this code or any regulation adopted pursuant to this code to keep the information required by subdivision (a) shall afford current and former employees the right to inspect or receive a copy of records pertaining to their employment, upon reasonable request to the employer. The employer may take reasonable steps to ensure the identity of a current or former employee. If the employer provides copies of the records, the actual cost of reproduction may be charged to the current or former employee."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 226(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=226.)
  "An employer who receives a written or oral request to inspect or receive a copy of records pursuant to subdivision (b) pertaining to a current or former employee shall comply with the request as soon as practicable, but no later than 21 calendar days from the date of the request. A violation of this subdivision is an infraction. Impossibility of performance, not caused by or a result of a violation of law, shall be an affirmative defense for an employer in any action alleging a violation of this subdivision. An employer may designate the person to whom a request under this subdivision will be made."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 226(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=226.)
  "A failure by an employer to permit a current or former employee to inspect or receive a copy of records within the time set forth in subdivision (c) entitles the current or former employee or the Labor Commissioner to recover a seven-hundred-fifty-dollar ($750) penalty from the employer."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 226(f) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=226.)

REMEDIES FOR NONCOMPLIANCE UNDER § 1198.5: $750 PENALTY, INJUNCTIVE RELIEF, AND INFRACTION STATUS
If Acme, Inc. fails to permit Jordan Lee (or Jordan Lee's representative) to inspect or copy personnel records within the time Labor Code § 1198.5 allows — including a time agreed to in writing under that statute — California law lets Jordan Lee, or separately the Labor Commissioner, recover a $750 penalty from Acme, Inc. Jordan Lee may also bring a civil action for injunctive relief to obtain compliance with § 1198.5, and may recover costs and reasonable attorney's fees in that action. Separately, a violation of § 1198.5 is an infraction, though "impossibility of performance," not caused by or resulting from a violation of law, is available to Acme, Inc. as an affirmative defense in any action alleging a violation of the statute.

  — Cal. Labor Code § 1198.5(k) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1198.5.)
  "A current or former employee may also bring an action for injunctive relief to obtain compliance with this section, and may recover costs and reasonable attorney’s fees in such an action."

CLOSING AND SIGNATURE
Please direct compliance with this request — inspection, copies, or both, as identified above — to Jordan Lee using the contact information provided below. If the records requested are not made available within the applicable statutory deadline described in this document, Jordan Lee reserves all rights and remedies available under California law, including the statutory penalties and civil remedies described above.

Sincerely,

Jordan Lee
Date: September 1, 2026
